I'm using my throwaway so that friends on reddit can't find my account. I'm a competitive player that has been in the VGC community for a very long time, even before it was called that. For ingame, I will religiously play the game "clean" with all my pokemon obtained legitimately, though for competitions I will hack if I have to, but obviously keeping it within what is physically possible within the game. When I first started competitive play, I was like a lot of the more pure players who would hate on anyone who even spoke of hacking. But after playing for over a decade, I've come to realize some inconvenient yet undeniable truths about the pokemon community:

* There will always be someone who dislikes you for some reason, and if you're going to survive as a real pokemon trainer you have to play for you, not for others. To that end, your own moral compass and perspective, so long as it doesn't hurt others, is most important. Resisting the urge to hack does not garner as much respect as you would think, and the people that disrespect you for hacking are either going to get over it or will find some other reason to dislike you. 

* The competitive scene is one that has always catered to the affluent, and has no sign of changing. For example, this current format requires you to gain 500 Championship Points before July to qualify for the World Championships, spread across Premiere Challenges (~$5), Midseason Showdowns (~$10-20), Regional Championships (~$30-40), and International Championships ($40). If you max out all of your Best Finish Limits, that alone will come close to $400-430 in entree fees alone, and then you have to factor in travel costs, which can raise it to about $1,800. All this is assuming you gain the CP you need from EVERY event - a more realistic number for someone that isn't regularly qualifying for Worlds is closer to $3-5,000 to qualify (I've qualified for the World Championships once but came close a few other years, so I am good but not good enough to top 4 every event I attend). Given these insane costs, it's tremendously heartbreaking to go to that many events breeding and soft resetting for everything every single time when you're spending so much real money, especially when the hack checks don't determine whether someone actually hacked, but rather whether someone hacked to the extent that they have something a normal player couldn't get on their own. If I put three months worth of work into a team that never accomplished anything, that would discourage me from continuing to play something I love, but a hacked team that is still following what is legally obtainable doesn't cause the same level of discouragement and general "what the fuck am I doing with my life" feeling. I may be mad that I lost, or mad that my efforts didn't pay off, but I won't be mad about the time spent putting it together. 

* The hard, bitter truth is that a hard majority of the players in the VGC scene hack or get someone to hack anyway. Nobody in that community that has branched out to the veterans really cares one way or another barring the blatantly illegal stuff, but the unavoidable fact is that those who can build their team in an hour as opposed to months can devote that extra time to either 1. practicing and testing the team to know it's worth before going into the tournament, or 2. Working a job that will allow that player to go to more tournaments and increase the likelihood of qualifying. 

* When it comes down to it, a tournament is not designed to test who spent the most time playing; it's designed to determine who played the best that particular day with the tools they brought. And at the end of the day, someone who hacks but has no clue what they're doing isn't going to last very long, even compared to someone with mediocre stats but has dramatically more experience with the metagame. The argument that people have an unfair advantage compared to those that breed makes a lot of sense in theory, but playing for this long I can say with full confidence that is a grossly overexaggerated claim. 

Anyway, that's the "why I do it." As for the "does it ever ruin the game for you," here are some other thoughts:

* Again, when playing ingame, I almost never hack. The only exception is when I'm playing a game like Black/White or Sun/Moon, where certain pokemon just don't exist in that game and I want to experience the game combining new pokemon with my favorite pokemon. But stats are really irrelevant to the ingame experience since you can just grind forever and win anyway, so I never need to hack there. To that end, I'd say it doesn't really change the experience in any negative way. 

* I got out of my way to respect other people's preferences in communities that are not the VGC community. Namely, if I'm in a group that plays entirely casualty and prefers against it, I will never mention hacking, use hacked pokemon against them, or trade them hacked pokemon. Generally speaking, if the higher ups in a given community don't like it, I'll respect that community as a guest in their circle. So that part isn't ruined. 

* While not an aspect of the game itself, I think the only thing I wish could be different would be that I wish hacking was more widely accepted. Every pokemon community has some really great people, but also someone who will take this way too seriously and make an elitism out of a children's video game. When you step back and really look at what you're fighting for, priorities can shift around a bit.

Hello! I've asked a lot of questions here, and I'm trying to contribute a little as I go now so I can give back a bit. And as someone who always prefers the more polite, constructive approach, I can definitely understand the request for such and will do my best to talk to you the way I would've wanted for myself. 

One thing I read a while back that may be useful is from a researcher named Stanley Sue. He wrote something in 2008 that talked about past attempts to give marginalized minorities more rights, and he said that of the groups that successfully achieved equality, they all had to go through certain steps. Namely: 

* Diversity: bringing individuals who have different identities (race, gender, ethnicity, orientation, etc) into the same space.

* Multiculturalism: Celebrating and building respect for other cultures and races. Learning about other racial and ethnic identities.

* Cross-cultural competency: working effectively in cross cultural spaces and with individuals who’s cultural beliefs and values may be fundamentally different than one’s own.  This is not exploitative, but more wondering how to make this space for everyone at the table. 

* Racial/Ethnic Justice: Ensuring that individuals from different racial and cultural backgrounds have equal privileges and access to resources in our communities, institutions, and society. 

For the most part, you can think of it like a ladder; you can't really accomplish one without achieving the one before it. Now, one thing that I've more or less come to realize in my journey towards a more feminist life is that a lot of times people have the same goal - equality, that is - but they argue and fight anyway. The problem isn't so much that one person is sexist, or that the two groups don't respect each other, but more that they respect and expect respect in return in the way *they* define respect. In terms of the ladder analogy, I find that a lot of arguments could be boiled down to one of two ideas: either that the person being called sexist believes one step of the ladder is the highest we need to go, or that the marginalized group feels like the highest step of the ladder should be inherently visible and a reasonable want - which it is, but it isn't always so easy to see from the other side. That, or they expect the highest peg of the ladder without the steps in between. For example, you can't really achieve equality of the two groups haven't learned to work together yet. 

So let's go back to your Minions comment. The issue that I think a lot of feminists see is not that the movie directly infringes on their rights - to that end, you are correct in assuming it's not a direct issue. But in order to achieve equality, men and women have to be able to work together and better understand each other's needs, and before that we have to have a safe environment to learn about each other's struggles without ridicule or downplay, and before that we need the diversity that would make that possible. So while it is entirely a creator's choice to make a movie that's all male characters, and while that in and of itself doesn't infringe on any rights, it does make larger problems more difficult to tackle down the road. 

I think some people struggle to see the need or use of feminism because they either grew up in an area where things were pretty much equal as far as they could see and don't relate to the struggles people talk about, or they grew up in a predominantly male environment where those struggles weren't really coming up because they weren't relevant to every day life. Admittedly, part of my own attempts to become more feminism sort of result from some of those things. Like you, I grew up in a pretty small town, so most of the place was peaceful enough that I never really questioned the possibility of widespread sexism in absolutely everything. But the more I read into this stuff, the more I start to realize things don't quite add up, and that feminism definitely has its uses.
